_about: Concept ladder for the Learn stage. One concept per rung. Rung ids are progress keys: never rename. skills are glossary.json ids that move to Practiced when the check is passed. goals maps checkpoint data-ids to the rungs (1-based) that teach them. lang: c programs are compiled and run to verify each check.

rungs.title: Your first C program
rungs.builds: Environment Setup: VS Code open on your exercises folder, and cl working.
rungs.why: Every C program you’ll write, the game included, has the same skeleton: pull in the tools you need, start at main, do the work, report that it finished. Learn the skeleton once and every file after this looks familiar.

parts: Three kinds of line

Every line in this program is one of three things, and knowing which is half of reading C.

  • A directive starts with #. It isn't really C: it's a note to a tool that runs before the compiler. #include <stdio.h> means “paste in the description of the input/output tools here”. A directive takes up one line and never ends with ;.
  • A function is a named block of code. main is the one every program must have, because Windows starts your program by running it.
  • A statement is one instruction inside a function, like printf(...); or return 0;. Statements run top to bottom and each one ends with ;.
Why the semicolon?

C doesn't care about line breaks, so you could spread one statement over three lines or put two on one line. The ; is how the compiler knows where each instruction stops. Directives don't need one because a directive always ends at the end of its line.

Put a ; after #include <stdio.h> and MSVC warns about unexpected tokens (C4067). With the warnings-as-errors flag you add in build.bat and compiler flags, that stops the build.
Calling a function

printf("Hello\n"); calls printf: it asks a function someone else wrote to do its job. The brackets hold what you hand over, here a piece of text. Text in double quotes is called a string literal. The quotes mark where it starts and ends; they aren't printed.

printf prints exactly what you give it and nothing more. It never moves to a new line by itself, so printf("Game "); printf("over\n"); prints one line: Game over.
Spelling matters
C is case-sensitive. main, Main and MAIN are three different names, and only the first one starts your program. Printf is not printf either.
What return 0 does

return 0; does two jobs at once: it ends main, which ends the program, and it hands Windows the number 0, meaning “finished fine”. Since C99 a program that reaches the closing } of main returns 0 anyway, but writing it says what you mean. You'll see that number again when build.bat checks it.
Why int main(void)?
int is the kind of value main hands back (a whole number). (void) says it takes nothing in. Older code writes int main(), which works too; from C23 the two mean the same thing.

walk: #include <stdio.h> pulls in the standard input/output toolbox. printf lives there. Leave it out and MSVC warns that printf is undeclared (C4013). With the warnings-as-errors flag you add in build.bat and compiler flags, that stops the build.
main is where every C program starts. int means it hands back a whole number when it finishes. (void) means it takes nothing in. The { opens its body.
printf prints the text between the quotes. The \n moves to a new line. The ; ends the statement, like a full stop.
Statements run top to bottom, one after another.
return 0 tells Windows “finished, no problems”. Any other number means something went wrong.
The } closes main. Every { needs a matching }.
rungs.model: Mental model: a recipe card. #include lists the tools, main is “start here”, each line inside is one step, and return 0 is “done”.

opts: Nothing until you add a third printf
check.hint: Each \n is a press of Enter. How many lines does that make?
check.why: Two lines. Each \n ends a line, so “Ready to ship.” starts on the next one. The backslash and n are never printed themselves.

miss.0: \n is an instruction to start a new line, not text to print.
miss.1: That would need the \n removed from the first printf.
miss.3: Two printf calls are enough. Each one runs and prints.

tryit.task: Add a third line that prints your name. Compile and run it: the next concept shows exactly how.
tryit.answer: printf("Sam\n");   any text inside the quotes, ending with \n

qa: Why int main(void)? What are the int and the void?

main hands a number back to Windows when it ends: 0 for success. int says what kind of thing it returns. void inside the brackets says it takes no inputs. You’ll see int main() in older code and it works, but (void) says exactly what you mean. Phase 3 covers inputs and return values properly.
What happens if I forget the ;?
The compiler stops with an error that usually points at the line after the one missing it. Reading compiler errors is all about reading those.
Does the spacing matter?
Mostly not. Indenting the lines inside { } is for you: it shows what belongs to main at a glance. Comments and layout covers the few places where a space does matter.
What does the .h in stdio.h mean?

It is a header. It holds a promise: a function called printf exists and this is how you call it. The compiler checks your calls against that promise, and the real code is added later when the program is linked. Phase 3.75 has you write your own header.
Why is the compiler so strict about a missing ; or a misspelled name?

The computer only understands machine code, and the compiler has to translate with no guessing. It stops rather than produce something wrong, which catches mistakes before they become bugs in a running game.
rungs.bridge: You can write a program. Next: turning it into something Windows can run, with cl.

rungs.title: Compiling and running with cl
rungs.builds: Your first C program: hello_world.c, saved in your p01 folder.
rungs.why: Windows can’t run hello_world.c. It’s text for humans. The compiler, cl, translates it into hello_world.exe, which Windows can run. Every change needs a fresh compile before you see it.

parts: Three jobs in one command

cl hello_world.c looks like one step, but it runs three in a row.

  1. Preprocess. Every # line is handled first. #include <stdio.h> is replaced by the whole text of stdio.h.
  2. Compile. Your C is translated into machine code and saved as hello_world.obj. Each call to printf is left as a gap marked “printf goes here”.
  3. Link. The linker joins your .obj to the C library that holds the real printf, fills the gaps and writes hello_world.exe.
Reading what cl prints

The output follows the same steps. A line with just hello_world.c means preprocessing and compiling ran. Then a Microsoft (R) Incremental Linker banner and /out:hello_world.exe mean linking ran. If an error stops the compile step, you never see the linker lines, and no new .exe is made.
See the pasted-in header

Run cl /P hello_world.c and cl stops after preprocessing. It writes hello_world.i: your program with stdio.h pasted in above it, hundreds of lines long. Your main is at the very bottom. Delete the .i when you're done looking.
Naming the .exe
The .exe is named after the first .c file on the line. /Fe:runner.exe picks a different name, and build.bat and compiler flags puts that in a script for you.
Why the command line?

Visual Studio's Build button runs the same cl underneath, hidden behind project settings. Typing it yourself means you see every step and every flag. When something breaks, you know which step broke, and the same commands drop straight into build.bat.

walk: cd moves the terminal into your project folder. cl looks for files in the folder you’re in.
dir lists the files here. Check hello_world.c is in the list before compiling.
cl reads hello_world.c and, if there are no errors, writes hello_world.obj and hello_world.exe next to it.
Typing the .exe name runs it. Its printf output appears right here in the terminal.
rungs.model: Mental model: the .c file is a recipe, cl is the cook, the .exe is the meal. Change the recipe and nothing happens until the cook makes it again.

check.q: You change “Hello” to “Hi” in hello_world.c, save, and run hello_world.exe again without running cl. What prints?
opts: An error: the .exe is out of date
check.hint: Which file did you change, and which file did you run?
check.why: The .exe is still the old build. It only changes when cl rebuilds it, so you see Hello, World! until you compile again. Forgetting to rebuild is the classic “my change didn’t work” moment.

miss.1: The .c file says Hi, but the .exe was built before the change.
miss.2: Windows doesn’t know or care that the .c changed. It just runs the old .exe.
miss.3: The old .exe still works. It just has the old text.

tryit.task: Fill in the commands: go to your p01 folder, compile greet.c, run it.
tryit.answer: cd …   then   cl greet.c   then   greet.exe

qa: 'cl' is not recognized
You’re in a terminal that hasn’t loaded Visual Studio’s tools. Use the Developer Command Prompt, or set up the VS Code terminal profile from Environment Setup step 8.
What is the .obj file?
A halfway step: your code compiled but not yet linked into a program. Phase 3.75 explains linking. You can ignore it for now.
Can I name the .exe something else?
Yes. Add /Fe:name.exe to the cl line. build.bat and compiler flags puts it in a script, so you never have to type it.
Why does C need a compile step when Python just runs?

Python works out what each line means while it runs. C does that work once up front: cl turns the whole file into machine code, so the .exe runs with no translator in the way. That speed is a big reason games are written in C and C++. The price is the wait and the strictness.
What is actually inside hello_world.exe?
Machine code for your main, plus startup code from the C runtime. printf itself is not in your file: cl compiles your code to a .obj, then links it with the library that contains printf.
rungs.bridge: You can build and run. Next: comments and layout: notes the compiler skips, and where spaces matter.

rungs.title: Comments and layout
rungs.builds: Your first C program: the shape of a .c file. Compiling and running with cl: what happens before your code is translated.
rungs.why: Code gets read far more often than it gets written, mostly by future you. Comments let you leave notes in the file that the compiler skips, and layout makes the shape of the program obvious at a glance. The starter code is full of // TODO notes: this is what they are.

parts: Notes the compiler skips

A comment is text in your .c file that's for people, not the compiler. It's removed before your code is translated, so it can say anything. C has two kinds:

  • // note runs from the two slashes to the end of that line.
  • /* note */ runs from /* to the next */, however many lines that takes.

Comments have three everyday jobs: a header at the top saying what the file is, a note on a line explaining why it's there, and switching code off for a while without deleting it. That last one is called commenting out.
Block comments don't nest

A /* comment ends at the very first */ the compiler meets. Wrap a block that already holds a /* */ note, and your outer comment stops early, at the inner */. The rest of the code you meant to switch off is live again, followed by a stray */ that won't compile. To switch off code that contains block comments, put // on each line instead.
The comment that never closes

Forget the */ and the comment swallows everything after it: every printf, the return 0;, the closing brace. The compiler reaches the end of the file still inside the comment.

MSVC reports this as C1071: unexpected end of file found in comment. If an error points at the last line of the file, look upwards for a /* with no partner.
Where spaces matter

Before compiling, C splits your code into tokens: the smallest pieces that mean something, like int, main, (, 3, ; or a whole string literal. Between tokens you can add spaces, tabs and blank lines freely. Inside one you can't: re turn is two unknown names, not return.

A string literal is one token, and it must close on the line it opened. To spread long text over two lines, close the quotes and start a fresh string on the next line. C glues neighbouring strings into one.

A string with no closing quote before the end of its line is MSVC C2001: newline in constant.
Layout is for you

Since spacing between tokens is free, use it to show structure. Indent everything inside { } by four spaces, put one statement on each line, and leave a blank line between groups of steps. The compiler won't notice, but you'll spot a missing brace in seconds.

In VS Code, Ctrl+/ adds or removes // on every selected line, and Shift+Alt+A wraps the selection in /* */.

walk: /* starts a block comment and */ ends it. Everything between is skipped, even across several lines. A note at the top saying what the file does is a good habit.
// starts a line comment. The compiler skips from there to the end of the line.
Everything inside main is indented four spaces, so you can see at a glance what belongs to it. The compiler doesn't care; you do.
Code first, note after. The printf runs; the text after // doesn't. A good note says why, not what.
Commenting out: wrapping real code in a comment switches it off without deleting it. This printf never runs.
A string can't run past the end of its line. So close the quotes here...
...and open new ones on the next line. Two strings side by side join into one, so this prints Press any key to start.
rungs.model: Mental model: comments are sticky notes on a recipe card. The cook reads round them. Layout is the handwriting: neat or messy, the recipe is the same, but only neat is easy to follow.

opts:
RUNNER
Lives: 3
Press any key to start

RUNNER
Lives: 3
Cheat mode on
Press any key to start

RUNNER
Lives: 3   three, so one mistake isn't game over
Press any key to start
Nothing: the string split over lines 13 and 14 is an error
check.hint: Which lines does the compiler actually see once the comments are gone?
check.why: Comments are removed before your code is translated, so the cheat line and the note on line 10 never reach the program. Lines 13 and 14 are two complete strings side by side, and C joins them into one.

miss.1: Line 11 is inside /* */, so it's switched off.
miss.2: Everything after // is a note for you. printf never sees it.
miss.3: Each line has its own complete string, both quotes included. Splitting is only an error when one string has no closing quote before its line ends.

tryit.task: This won't compile, because the note on line 4 isn't marked as a comment. Fix it two ways: once with //, once with /* */.
tryit.answer: // show the starting score   or   /* show the starting score */

qa: Do comments make the .exe bigger or slower?
No. They're stripped out before your code is translated, so the .exe is identical with or without them. Comment as much as helps you.
Which should I use, // or /* */?
// for short notes, /* */ for a file header or a longer explanation. Very old C (C89) only had /* */, which is why older code uses it everywhere.
What's worth writing in a comment?
Why, not what. printf("Lives: 3\n"); // print lives tells you nothing the code doesn't. // three, so one mistake isn't game over records a decision you'd otherwise forget.
Is // inside a string a comment?
No. Inside double quotes it's just text: printf("a // b\n"); prints a // b.
rungs.bridge: You can make code readable. Next: escape sequences and %d, controlling exactly what printf shows.

rungs.title: Escape sequences and %d
rungs.builds: Your first C program: printf and \n. Comments and layout: a string literal is one token. Session 1: the disappearing “Lets”.
rungs.why: Some characters can’t be typed straight into a string: a new line, a tab, a quote. C uses a backslash to say “the next character is special”. And %d drops a number into your text, which is how the game will show a score.

parts: The format string

The first thing you hand printf is the format string: the text in quotes that says what to print. Most of it is printed exactly as written. Two characters are special. \ starts an escape sequence, and % starts a conversion specification, a slot like %d that a value will fill.

It's called a conversion because the value isn't stored as text. The number 120 sits in memory as binary, and %d tells printf to turn it into the characters 1, 2 and 0.
Slots fill in order

Each value after the format string goes into the next slot, left to right. printf("Wave %d of %d\n", 2, 5); prints Wave 2 of 5. Swap the 2 and the 5 and you get Wave 5 of 2. printf can't know what you meant, only the order you gave.
Two tools, two times

Escapes and slots look alike, but different tools handle them at different times.

  • \n, \t, \\ and \" are swapped for single characters by the compiler, while it builds the .exe. By the time the program runs, the backslash is long gone.
  • %d and %% are read by printf each time it runs, when it has the actual values.

That's why \% doesn't print a percent sign: it isn't an escape C knows (C4129), so only printf's %% works.
A few more escapes

\a asks the terminal to beep, though many stay silent. \b moves the cursor back one place, so the next character overwrites the last one. \t jumps to the next tab stop, but where the stops are is up to the terminal, usually every 8 columns. Line up a scoreboard with tabs and it may look different on another machine.
Mistakes MSVC catches

Count your slots and your values. In plain C a mismatch compiles and prints garbage. Under our /W4 /WX build, MSVC checks every printf whose format string is written in the call, and stops the build instead:

  • more slots than values: C4473
  • more values than slots: C4474
  • a value of the wrong type for its slot: C4477
  • a backslash escape C doesn't know, like \q: C4129

Windows paths are the classic C4129. "C:\Games" contains \G, which isn't an escape. Double every backslash: "C:\\Games".

walk: \t is a tab: a jump to the next column. %d is a slot that gets filled with 120.
\\ prints one backslash. You need two, because a single \ starts an escape.
%% prints one percent sign. A single % would start a slot like %d.
\r jumps back to the start of the line without moving down, so “ party” writes over “Lets”. You saw this in Session 1.
rungs.model: Mental model: inside the quotes, \ and % are control keys. \ controls the cursor, % opens a slot. To print either one as plain text, press it twice.

check.q: What does line 7 show on screen?
check.hint: \r moves the cursor back to the start of the same line. What happens to “Lets”?
check.why: “Lets” prints, \r sends the cursor back to the start of the line, and “ party” is written over it. It’s six characters long, so it covers all four letters of Lets.

miss.0: \r goes back to the start of the same line. \n is the one that moves down.
miss.1: \r doesn’t print anything. It moves the cursor back, and the next text overwrites.
miss.2: Close, but there’s only one space before party in the code, so only one space is printed before it.

qa: How do I print a double quote?
Escape it: \" inside the string. printf("She said \"hi\"\n");
What other escapes are there?
\t (tab), \\ (backslash), \" (quote), \' (single quote) and \0, the end of a string, which Phase 3 explains. \n and \t are the ones you’ll use most.
Can %d show a decimal number?
No. %d is for whole numbers only. Phase 2 adds %f for decimals.
Is \r ever useful, or was it just a Session 1 accident?
It is the oldest trick in terminal drawing. In Phase 4.5 you will use it on purpose to redraw the game over the same line every frame.
Why does my prompt appear glued to the end of my output?
printf never adds a new line for you. Add \n to the last printf and the prompt starts on its own line.
rungs.bridge: You can print text and a fixed number. Next: variables: storing a number, so %d can show a score that changes.

rungs.title: Variables: storing a number
rungs.kick: int · declare · = · %d with a value · names
rungs.builds: Escape sequences and %d: each %d slot takes the next value. Your first C program: statements run top to bottom.
rungs.why: A game is mostly numbers that change: the score goes up, lives go down, the level ticks over. A variable is a named box that holds one of those numbers, so your code can store it, change it and print it. Until now %d could only show a number you typed in. Now it shows whatever the box holds.

parts: A named box

A variable is a named piece of memory that holds one value. In this phase every variable is an int: a whole number such as 0, 3 or −250. Decimals and letters need other types, which Variables and types in Phase 2 covers.
Declare, assign, initialise

Three words, three steps:

  • Declare: int score; makes a box called score. It has a name and a type, but no value you can rely on.
  • Assign: score = 0; stores 0 in it.
  • Initialise: int lives = 3; declares the box and gives it a first value in one line.

Initialising is the habit to build. A box that's never empty can't surprise you.
= stores, it doesn't compare

In maths, = says two sides are equal. In C it's an instruction: work out the right side, then put the result in the variable on the left. So score = score + 10; is fine. It reads the old score, adds 10 and stores the new total. The left side has to be a variable; 10 = score; won't compile.
Printing values

Now %d earns its place. Each %d in the format string is filled by the next value after it, and that value can be a variable or a sum:

printf("Lives: %d
", lives);
printf("%d of %d
", score, 1000);
printf("Next: %d
", level + 1);

Anything that works out to a value, like level + 1, is called an expression. The last line works out level + 1 and prints the answer. level doesn't change: only = changes a variable.
Naming rules

A name you make up is called an identifier. It can use letters, digits and _, but can't start with a digit. lives, enemy_count and wave2 are fine; 2lives and enemy-count aren't. Names are case-sensitive, so Score and score are two different boxes.

You can't use a keyword, one of C's own words, as a name: int, return, if, while, for, void, char and a few dozen more. Avoid names starting with an underscore too, because the compiler and its libraries use those. Pick names that say what the number is: lives beats x.
Mistakes that bite

• Using a box before filling it. An int you never assigned holds whatever was left in that memory: garbage.
  • Thinking int a, b = 0; sets both. It sets only b.
  • Misspelling the name. scroe isn't score, and the compiler has never heard of it.

MSVC warns when you read a variable before giving it a value (C4700), and /WX turns that into a failed build. A misspelled or undeclared name is error C2065: undeclared identifier. You'll meet both again in Reading compiler errors.

walk: int score; is a declaration: make a box called score that holds a whole number. Nothing in it yet is worth trusting.
Declare and initialise in one line: lives is made and holds 3 from the start.
Assignment: = stores the value on the right in the box on the left. score now holds 0.
%d is filled with whatever score holds right now: 0.
Assigning again replaces the old value. The 0 is gone; score is 250.
Two slots, two values, filled in order: score, then lives.
level + 1 is worked out (2) and printed. level itself still holds 1.
rungs.model: Mental model: a labelled box on a shelf. The label is the name, the box holds exactly one whole number, and putting a new number in throws the old one out.

check.q: After line 13 runs, what does level hold?
opts: Nothing: printing it used it up
check.hint: Does line 13 store anything in level, or only read it?
check.why: Only = changes a variable. level + 1 reads level, works out 2 and hands that to printf. The box still holds 1.

miss.1: printf shows 2, but that's the value of the expression. Nothing stored it back in level.
miss.2: level was initialised to 1 on line 6, and nothing has stored anything else in it since.
miss.3: Reading a variable never empties it. You can print it as often as you like.

tryit.task: Make a box called coins holding 5, then print Coins: 5 using it.

qa: What does int a, b = 0; set?
Only b. The = 0 belongs to b alone; a is declared but holds garbage. Write int a = 0, b = 0;, or more clearly, one declaration per line.
Isn't score = score + 10 a maths mistake?

In maths it would be. In C, = means store. The right side is worked out first using the old score, then the result goes back into score, so it adds 10. Comparing two values uses ==, which Decisions with if / else covers in Phase 2.5.
Why do I get C4700 when I print a variable?
You read it before storing anything in it. Give it a value when you declare it: int score = 0;.
How big a number can an int hold?
On Windows, from about −2.1 billion to +2.1 billion. Variables and types in Phase 2 covers sizes, decimals (float) and single characters (char).
Do declarations have to go at the top?
No. Since C99 you can declare a variable anywhere in main before you use it. Grouping them at the top, as here, keeps them easy to find. Very old C required it.
rungs.bridge: You can store and print numbers. Next: reading compiler errors, including the ones a mistyped variable name causes.

rungs.title: Reading compiler errors
rungs.builds: Your first C program: every statement ends with ;. Compiling and running with cl: cl reports problems when you compile. Variables: storing a number: every name must be declared.
rungs.why: You will see compiler errors every day, for as long as you write code. They look scary but follow one pattern: file, line, code, message. Reading them calmly is a skill, and it’s the fastest way to fix your own code.

parts: Errors and warnings

An error means your code breaks C's rules, so the compiler can't translate it. A warning means the code is legal but looks like a mistake. C was built to be small and fast, and it trusts you to mean what you write, so very little gets checked while the program runs. Warnings are the compiler's chance to catch you first, which is why our build treats them as errors.
How to read one

Every message has four parts: file(line): error C2143: message. Fix the first one, rebuild, and repeat. Later messages are often knock-on effects. If the line it names looks fine, check the line above.
The ones Phase 1 produces

C2143  missing ';' before ...    the line above lacks its ;
C2001  newline in constant        a string never closed
C2017  illegal escape sequence    \n outside the quotes
C4013  'prinf' undefined          misspelled function name;
       then LNK2019               without /WX, the link fails
C1071  end of file in comment     a /* with no */
C4700  uninitialized variable     read before it was set
C2065  undeclared identifier      variable misspelled or
                                  never declared
What the codes mean
C2xxx is an error and C4xxx a warning. C1xxx is fatal: the compiler gives up on the spot. LNKxxxx comes from the linker, after compiling worked.
The extra C2220 line
With build.bat's /WX, every warning comes with a second line: error C2220: the following warning is treated as an error. That line isn't a new problem. Read the warning next to it and fix that.

walk: This line is fine: it ends with ;.
The ; is missing at the end of this line. The compiler doesn’t complain yet.
It complains here, on reaching return without having seen a ;. cl prints hello_world.c(6): error C2143: syntax error: missing ';' before 'return'. That’s file, line, error code, message.
rungs.model: Mental model: the compiler reads like you do, top to bottom. It reports a problem at the first place it can’t make sense of things, which is often one line after the actual mistake.

check.q: The error says line 6. Where do you fix it?
opts: Line 5: add a ; at the end
Line 4: the first printf is wrong
check.hint: What does the message say is missing, and which statement should have ended with it?
check.why: The mistake is on line 5, the line before the one reported. The compiler only noticed when it reached return on line 6. When an error points at a line that looks fine, check the line above it.

miss.0: return 0; already has its ;. The message says the ; is missing before return.
miss.2: Line 4 is fine. It has its ;.
miss.3: The file name has nothing to do with it.

tryit.task: This has two mistakes. Build it, read the first error, fix it, build again, then fix the next.
tryit.answer: Line 4 is missing the ; at the end. Line 5 is missing the closing " before the ). Fix the first error first: one mistake can cause several messages.

qa: Error or warning: what’s the difference?

An error (C2xxx) means no .exe is made. A warning (C4xxx) means something looks wrong. On its own it still makes an .exe, but the build.bat in the next concept adds /WX, which turns every warning into an error, so no .exe either.
Why do I get ten errors for one mistake?
After the first problem the compiler gets confused about what follows. Fix the first error, rebuild, and many of the others disappear.
How do I look up an error code?
Search “MSVC C2143”. Microsoft’s page for each code explains it with examples.
Why does the error say \n is unknown, C2017?
The ended up outside the quotes. Write printf("text "), not printf("text") .
rungs.bridge: You can read the compiler’s complaints. Next: build.bat, one word that compiles with the right warnings switched on.

rungs.title: build.bat and compiler flags
rungs.builds: Compiling and running with cl: the cl command and /Fe:. Reading compiler errors: errors and warnings.
rungs.why: Typing cl with the right flags every time gets old, and it’s easy to forget the flags that catch bugs. build.bat is a file of commands you run with one word: build. Every project from here on has one.

parts: Make the compiler fussy

The best setting for a beginner is the strictest one. Every warning is the compiler pointing at a line that's probably wrong, for free. With MSVC that means /W4, the highest everyday warning level, plus /WX so none of them can be ignored.
Why not /Wall?

MSVC has a level above /W4 called /Wall. It switches on warnings that are off for good reason, many of them about Microsoft's own headers: padding inside structs, which functions got inlined. With /WX those would fail every build and tell you nothing useful. /W4 is what real projects use.
Sticking to the standard

C has an official rulebook, and its versions are named by year: C99, C11, C17. The flag /std:c17 tells cl to follow C17 rather than its own default. It's the first flag in FLAGS. The test build on your PC confirmed that cl, and even windows.h, compile cleanly with it.
ERRORLEVEL is main's return value

When a program ends, Windows keeps the number it returned in %ERRORLEVEL%. For your programs, that's the value after return in main. Run hello_world.exe, then echo %ERRORLEVEL%, and you'll see 0. cl plays by the same rule: 0 if the build worked, anything else if it didn't. Line 4 of build.bat checks exactly that.

A printf slot with no value, printf("%d\n"), is C4473. Under /WX that's BUILD FAILED, which is what you want.
learn.king: Chapter 1 and 2 Q&A on warning levels

walk: @echo off stops Windows printing each command before running it, so you only see the results.

set FLAGS= saves the compiler flags in one place. /std:c17 follows the C17 rulebook, /W4 turns on most warnings, /WX makes any warning stop the build, /Zi writes debug information into a .pdb file and /Od turns off optimisation, so the debugger (Phase 3.75) can follow your code line by line.
%FLAGS% is swapped for the flags. /Fe: names the .exe.
%ERRORLEVEL% holds the result of the last command: 0 means cl succeeded, anything else means it failed. neq means “not equal”.
Runs only if the build failed.
exit /b 1 stops the script and reports failure.
Only reached when cl succeeded.
rungs.model: Mental model: build.bat is a recipe card for the cook. You write the steps once, flags included, and every build follows them exactly.

check.q: hello_world.c has a printf("%d\n") with no number after it, so cl gives one warning (C4473) and nothing else is wrong. What does build print at the end?
check.why: /WX turns every warning into an error, so cl fails, %ERRORLEVEL% isn’t 0, and you get BUILD FAILED. That’s the point: warnings are bugs you haven’t met yet, and /WX won’t let you ignore them.

miss.0: Without /WX it would. With /WX, any warning fails the build.
miss.2: With /WX the warning becomes an error, so there’s no BUILD OK.
miss.3: The script always ends with BUILD OK or BUILD FAILED.

qa: Why does typing build work without .bat?
When you type a name, Windows tries .bat, .cmd and .exe automatically, as long as the file is in the current folder.
What is rem?
A comment line in a .bat file, like // in C. The longer build.bat in the full notes uses rem to explain every flag.
When do I add more .c files?
From Phase 3.75. You’ll list them in a SOURCES variable and pass them all to cl.
When do I switch /Od to /O2?
/Od switches optimisation off for faster builds while you develop. When you ship, use /O2 for a faster executable.
Should build.bat be committed?
Yes, it's part of the project. The files it produces (*.exe, *.obj, *.pdb) are not. Saving your work with Git, next, adds a three-line .gitignore for them.
rungs.bridge: You can build with one word. Last: saving your work to GitHub, so it’s backed up and your partner can see it.

rungs.title: Saving your work with Git
rungs.builds: Environment Setup: Git installed and your game-dev-exercises repo cloned.
rungs.why: Right now your code lives on one hard drive. Git takes snapshots of it, and GitHub keeps a copy online that Person A, your programming partner, can read. Small snapshots, often, mean you can always get back to a version that worked.

parts: The session loop

Git keeps a history of snapshots, called commits, on your machine. GitHub keeps a copy online. Every session follows the same loop: git pull to fetch anything new, do your work, then status, add, commit, push.
pull and log

git pull downloads commits from GitHub that you don't have yet, such as ones Person A pushed or ones you made on another computer, and merges them into your files. Run it before you start. git log --oneline lists your commits, newest first, one line each. It's how you check a commit really happened.
Why the practice commits name files

The Phase 1 tasks use git add hello_world.c build.bat, not git add .. The dot adds everything that changed, and every build leaves .exe, .obj and .pdb files behind. They're rebuilt from your code any time, they're large, and they change on every build. Naming files means only what you meant goes in, and you look at each one as you add it.
A three-line .gitignore

Better still, tell Git to skip build output for good. Make a file called .gitignore in the repo's top folder:

*.exe
*.obj
*.pdb

* means “any name”. Commit the .gitignore itself, and git status stops listing build files. Phase 4's .gitignore concept covers the rest.

If git push is rejected and mentions fetching first, GitHub has commits you don't. Run git pull, then push again.

rungs.code:
git status
git add hello_world.c build.bat
git commit -m "Add hello world and build.bat"
git push
walk: git status shows what changed since your last snapshot. Run it before and after everything.
git add picks the files for the next snapshot. Nothing is saved yet.
git commit takes the snapshot, with a message saying what changed. It’s saved on your machine only.
git push sends your snapshots to GitHub. Now they’re backed up and visible to Person A.
rungs.model: Mental model: add puts photos in an envelope, commit seals it with a label, push posts it. Nothing leaves your computer until the push.

check.q: You run git add and git commit, then your laptop dies. Is your work on GitHub?
check.hint: Which of the three commands actually talks to GitHub?
check.why: commit saves the snapshot on your machine. Only push sends it to GitHub. Commit, then push, every session.

miss.0: commit is local. It’s push that uploads.
miss.1: Nothing goes to GitHub until push, message included.
miss.2: add only picks files for a snapshot. Nothing goes online until push.

qa: What makes a good commit message?
Say what changed, as if finishing “This commit will…”: “Add build.bat”, “Fix warning C4244 in var()”. Phase 4 goes deeper.
git push asks me to sign in
The first push from a new computer opens a GitHub sign-in in your browser. After that it remembers you.
Should I commit the .exe?
No. It's rebuilt from your code any time. Add the three-line .gitignore from this page and Git skips .exe, .obj and .pdb files automatically.
Does the commit message need a format?
A tidy habit is type: short description, with types like feat, fix, refactor and docs, for example feat: hello world compiles and runs.
What does git add . do, and how do I confirm a push worked?

The dot means every changed file, build output included unless a .gitignore leaves it out. That's why the practice commits name each file. To confirm a push, run git log --oneline, or open github.com/4samtaylor/game-dev-exercises and refresh: your commit should be at the top.
